lessons.title: Group 2: the alkaline earth metals

objectives: Describe and explain trends in reactivity, hydroxide and sulfate solubility and thermal stability of Group 2 compounds
Write equations for reactions with oxygen, water, acids and for the thermal decomposition of carbonates and nitrates
Describe flame tests, tests for sulfate and uses of calcium and magnesium compounds
reviewNotes: Data used: Ar H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0, Na 23.0, Mg 24.0, Al 27.0, S 32.0, Cl 35.5, K 39.0, Ca 40.0, Fe 56.0, Cu 63.5, Zn 65.0, Ag 108.0, Ba 137.0; R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; molar volume 24.0 dm³ at room temperature and pressure; K_w = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
K_sp(Ca(OH)₂) = 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ is a typical textbook value. Use of lime in Cameroonian agriculture is stated generally; verify local practice.
Ionisation energies are standard values (Be 900, Mg 738, Ca 590, Sr 549, Ba 503 kJ mol⁻¹).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Reactions of Group 2 metals
blocks.md:
The atoms have two outer s electrons and form M²⁺ ions. Reactivity **increases down the group** because the first and second ionisation energies fall (larger atoms, more shielding, outer electrons further from the nucleus).

- With oxygen: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (Mg burns with a bright white flame).
- With water: Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but quickly with steam (MgO + H₂); Ca, Sr and Ba react with cold water giving M(OH)₂ + H₂, increasingly vigorously.
- With dilute acids: M + 2H⁺ → M²⁺ + H₂.

blocks.title: Trends in compounds
blocks.md:
- **Hydroxides**: solubility **increases** down the group (Mg(OH)₂ is almost insoluble, Ba(OH)₂ is soluble); limewater is Ca(OH)₂(aq).
- **Sulfates**: solubility **decreases** down the group (BaSO₄ is insoluble: used as the test for sulfate and as a 'barium meal').
- **Thermal stability** of carbonates and nitrates **increases** down the group: the smaller, more highly polarising M²⁺ distorts the anion and weakens it. MCO₃ → MO + CO₂; 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂.

blocks.caption: First ionisation energy of the Group 2 elements: it falls down the group, so reactivity rises.
blocks.alt: A bar chart of the first ionisation energy for beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium, decreasing from left to right.

blocks.title: Tests and uses
blocks.md:
**Flame tests**: Ca brick-red, Sr crimson, Ba apple-green (Mg gives none). **Sulfate test**: acidify with dilute HCl (removes carbonate), add BaCl₂(aq): white precipitate of BaSO₄.

Uses: **quicklime** CaO and **slaked lime** Ca(OH)₂ to neutralise acidic soil and in cement and mortar; limestone CaCO₃ in building and blast furnaces; **Mg(OH)₂** ('milk of magnesia') as an antacid; Mg alloys.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Explaining thermal stability by the size of the cation without mentioning polarisation of the anion.
- Saying that Mg(OH)₂ is soluble because it is a hydroxide of a metal: solubility rises down the group.
- Forgetting to acidify before adding barium chloride (carbonate would also precipitate).
- Writing the wrong formula for the nitrate: Ca(NO₃)₂ gives 4NO₂ for every 2 formula units.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Limewater
blocks.statement: K_sp for Ca(OH)₂ is 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ mol³ dm⁻⁹. Find the solubility and the pH of saturated limewater.
steps: pH = 14 − 1.65 = 12.35, so limewater is strongly alkaline.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Quicklime
blocks.statement: Limestone (90 % CaCO₃) is heated: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Find the mass of CaO from 50.0 kg of limestone (A_r: Ca 40, C 12, O 16).
steps: n(CaO) = 450 mol; M(CaO) = 56 g mol⁻¹.

blocks.title: Trends in the halogens
blocks.md:
At room temperature: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine a pale green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, iodine a grey-black solid (purple vapour). Melting and boiling points **increase** down the group (stronger London forces with more electrons).

The halogens are **oxidising agents**; the oxidising power **decreases** down the group (E°: F₂ +2.87, Cl₂ +1.36, Br₂ +1.07, I₂ +0.54 V) because the atom gains an electron less readily as it gets larger.

blocks.title: Displacement and halide ions
blocks.md:
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (orange solution); Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (brown; purple in hexane); Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.

**Halide reducing power increases down the group**: with concentrated H₂SO₄, NaCl gives only HCl (steamy fumes); NaBr gives HBr and also Br₂ and SO₂; NaI gives HI, I₂ and also S and H₂S. **AgNO₃(aq)**: AgCl white (dissolves in dilute NH₃), AgBr cream (in concentrated NH₃), AgI yellow (insoluble).

blocks.caption: Standard electrode potentials of the halogens: the oxidising power decreases down the group.
blocks.alt: A bar chart of E° for fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine, decreasing from 2.87 to 0.54 volts.

blocks.title: Chlorine and disproportionation
blocks.md:
Chlorine in water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO (chlorine is both oxidised and reduced): HClO disinfects water. Cold dilute NaOH: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (bleach, Cl: +1). Hot concentrated NaOH gives chlorate(V): 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.

**Iodine–thiosulfate titration**: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻ (starch indicator, blue-black → colourless). Used to find the oxidising agent that liberates iodine from excess KI.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that iodine is the strongest oxidising agent because it is the largest: it is the weakest.
- Forgetting that silver halide tests need dilute nitric acid first.
- Writing the products of H₂SO₄ + NaBr or NaI as only HBr and HI (these are further oxidised).
- Mixing up 'oxidised' and 'reduced' in disproportionation: the same element does both.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Bleach analysis
blocks.statement: 25.0 cm³ of diluted bleach liberates iodine from excess acidified KI: ClO⁻ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → Cl⁻ + I₂ + H₂O. The iodine needs 20.00 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Na₂S₂O₃. Find [ClO⁻] in the diluted bleach.
steps: Ratio ClO⁻ : I₂ = 1 : 1, so n(ClO⁻) = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol in 25.0 cm³.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Reactions of halide ions
blocks.statement: Predict the observations when chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution and the product is shaken with hexane.
steps: Cl₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than I₂ (E° 1.36 V against 0.54 V), so it oxidises I⁻: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂.
The aqueous layer turns brown (I₂ in water).
On shaking with hexane, iodine dissolves in the upper hexane layer, which turns purple.

blocks.title: Oxides
blocks.md:
Across period 3 the oxides change from ionic and basic to covalent and acidic:

- **Na₂O** (ionic, basic): Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (pH about 14). **MgO** (ionic, basic): slightly soluble; MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.
- **Al₂O₃** (ionic with covalent character, **amphoteric**): reacts with both acid and alkali.
- **SiO₂** (giant covalent, acidic): insoluble; reacts with hot concentrated NaOH.
- **P₄O₁₀, SO₂/SO₃** (simple molecular, acidic): P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

blocks.title: Amphoteric aluminium oxide and chlorides
blocks.md:
Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] (sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate).

**Chlorides**: NaCl and MgCl₂ are ionic and dissolve in water to give neutral or slightly acidic solutions; **AlCl₃** and the covalent chlorides **SiCl₄**, **PCl₃/PCl₅** are hydrolysed by water, giving HCl (steamy fumes) and an acidic solution: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl; PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl.

blocks.caption: Period 3 oxides change from basic (ionic) through amphoteric to acidic (covalent).
blocks.alt: Six boxes labelled Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀ and SO₃, coloured from basic through amphoteric to acidic, with an arrow showing increasing acidity.

blocks.title: Explaining the trend
blocks.md:
The difference in electronegativity between the element and oxygen (or chlorine) falls across the period: **large** (Na, Mg): ionic bonding, oxide ion O²⁻ reacts with water or H⁺ (basic); **small** (Si, P, S, Cl): covalent, the oxide reacts with water to give acid (non-metal oxides are acidic).

The melting points reflect the structure: ionic or giant covalent (high) and simple molecular (low).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that SiO₂ reacts readily with water: it is insoluble.
- Writing Al₂O₃ as 'acidic' or 'basic' only: it is amphoteric.
- Predicting that MgCl₂ is hydrolysed like AlCl₃: only partly (slightly acidic solution).
- Forgetting that SO₂ forms sulfurous acid H₂SO₃ (pH about 3) while SO₃ gives sulfuric acid.

blocks.title: Example 1 — pH of a basic oxide
blocks.statement: What mass of Na₂O must dissolve in water to make 1.0 dm³ of solution of pH 13 (A_r: Na 23, O 16)?
steps: pH 13 means pOH 1, so [OH⁻] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH: each mole of Na₂O gives 2 mol OH⁻, so n(Na₂O) = 0.050 mol.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Amphoteric behaviour
blocks.statement: Show that aluminium oxide is amphoteric by writing two equations, and explain why it is not typical of metal oxides.
steps: With acid: Al₂O₃ + 6H⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3H₂O (acts as a base).
With alkali: Al₂O₃ + 2OH⁻ + 3H₂O → 2[Al(OH)₄]⁻ (acts as an acid).
The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises O²⁻ strongly, giving a bond with significant covalent character.
blocks.answer: Reacts with both acids and alkalis

Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Transition elements
blocks.md:
A **transition element** forms at least one ion with a **partially filled d subshell** (Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ do not count). Features: variable oxidation states (the 4s and 3d electrons have similar energies), coloured compounds, complex ions, catalytic activity, paramagnetism.

Configurations: Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. Ions lose 4s electrons first: Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵, Cu²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁹, Zn²⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰ (colourless).

blocks.title: Complexes and colour
blocks.md:
A **complex ion** has a central metal ion bonded to **ligands** by dative covalent bonds (ligands have lone pairs: H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻, OH⁻; EDTA⁴⁻ is polydentate). The **coordination number** is the number of dative bonds: 6 (octahedral, e.g. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻), 4 (tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻, square planar), 2 (linear [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).

Colour: the ligands split the d orbitals; electrons absorb visible light to move between d orbitals and the **complementary colour** is seen. The colour changes with the ligand, oxidation state and coordination number.

blocks.caption: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: an octahedral complex with six water ligands around a copper(II) ion.
blocks.alt: A copper ion at the centre with six water molecules around it in an octahedral arrangement.

blocks.title: Reactions of aqueous ions
blocks.md:
With NaOH(aq): Cu²⁺ → blue precipitate Cu(OH)₂; Fe²⁺ → green precipitate (turns brown in air); Fe³⁺ → red-brown Fe(OH)₃; Cr³⁺ → green Cr(OH)₃ which dissolves in excess to give a green solution (amphoteric); Mn²⁺ → pale precipitate that darkens.

With NH₃(aq): the same precipitates form, but Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess to give a **deep blue** solution of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ (ligand exchange). Catalysis: Fe in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, Ni in hydrogenation.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Counting Zn or Sc as transition metals: their common ions have empty or full d subshells.
- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming ions.
- Forgetting the overall charge of a complex: it is the sum of the metal charge and the ligand charges.
- Saying that colour arises from the metal alone: the ligand matters.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Charge and configuration
blocks.statement: Find the oxidation number of iron in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and the number of d electrons in Cu²⁺ and Fe³⁺.
steps: Six CN⁻ ligands contribute −6; overall charge is −3, so Fe = −3 + 6 = +3.
Cu²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁹ (9 d electrons); Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵ (5 d electrons).
Zn²⁺ would be 3d¹⁰ and colourless because its d subshell is full.
blocks.answer: Fe is +3; Cu²⁺ has 9 d electrons, Fe³⁺ has 5

blocks.title: Example 2 — Dichromate titration
blocks.statement: 25.0 cm³ of iron(II) sulfate solution needs 24.0 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇ in acid: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6Fe³⁺. Find [Fe²⁺].
steps: [Fe²⁺] = 1.44 × 10⁻³/0.0250 = 0.0576 mol dm⁻³ (the orange dichromate turns green).
